scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that reaching an audience is a strength, then argues merit does not require wide understanding; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: People often dismiss a difficult painting or poem by saying that no one can understand it.
Some people argue that a work of art must be understandable to most people in order to have any merit.
I agree that art should try to communicate something, but I disagree that it must be widely understood to be valuable.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why reaching an audience matters

sentences.text: First, there is a fair point in the idea that art should reach an audience.
Art that communicates nothing to anyone risks becoming private and meaningless to all but its maker.
For example, a song or film that moves millions of people clearly has a powerful kind of merit.
This shows that the ability to connect with an audience can be a real artistic strength.
Works that speak to ordinary people can comfort, inspire, and bring whole communities together.
An art that no one could ever respond to would struggle to matter at all.
To this extent, being understandable can genuinely add to a work's value.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why merit needs no majority

sentences.text: Second, however, demanding that art be understandable to most people sets a mistaken standard.
Many great works were strange or difficult at first and were understood only by a few.
Consider paintings or symphonies once mocked as confusing, which are now treasured as masterpieces.
Such cases show that difficulty is not the same as worthlessness, and time often reveals hidden depth.
Challenging art can stretch the imagination precisely because it is not instantly easy.
Judging merit by popularity would also reward the simple and familiar while punishing the bold and new.
Real artistic value, then, does not depend on being understood by the majority.
In conclusion, art that reaches many people has a genuine and valuable kind of merit.
But difficult works that few understand can be just as great, or even greater.
The worth of art lies in its depth and power, not simply in how many people grasp it at once.
